CPA and TG inhibit Ca2+ sequestering by the SR and that this results in decreased Ca2+ current amplitude, reduced SR Ca2+ loading and a decrease in the contraction.

cyclopiazonic-acid and thapsigargen inhibit the SR calcium pump and that this inhibition leads to a reduced Ca2+-induced calcium release and thereby to a reduced activation of L-type calcium channels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of Ca2+ currents in skeletal muscle fibres by the SR Ca2+-ATPase and the ryanodine receptor.
the regulation of Ca2+ channels by the RyRs in frog skeletal muscle.
the regulation of the calcium release channel in the sarcoplasmatic reticulum of frog skeletal muscle fibre.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RyR is a retrograde modulator of the L-type Ca2 channel, but the mechanism of this modulation is not clear.
cyclopiazonic and thapsigargenic acid, at concentrations that only partially inhibit SR Ca2+ uptake, reduce the Ca2+ loading and the Ca2+ content of the SR.
the RyR are the retrograde modulator of the L-type Ca(2+).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the RyR is a Ca2+-dependent regulator of the skeletal muscle dihydropyri-dine receptor.
the SR plays an important role in controlling the L-type Ca2+-current in frog skeletal muscle.
the Ca2+ release from the SR is a key factor in determining the activity of the L-type Ca2 channels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RyR are able to control L-type Ca2+-channel activity.
the SR Ca2+-ATPase is a target of CPA and TG in frog muscle fibres, and that CPA and TG reduce SR Ca2+ loading and Ca2+ currents in a concentration-dependent manner.
the Ca2+ release-dependent regulation of Ca2+ currents is a property of skeletal muscle fibres and that it can be modulated by drugs which selectively inhibit the SR Ca2+-ATPase.
